content: Hydrochlorides are chemical salts that are formed as a result of the reaction between hydrochloric acid and an organic base, most commonly amines. This type of compound is also referred to as muriate, a term derived from the alternative name for hydrochloric acid, muriatic acid. For instance, when pyridine (C₅H₅N) reacts with hydrochloric acid (HCl), the product is pyridine hydrochloride (C₅H₅N·HCl). However, the use of a dot in this formula is misleading, as it incorrectly suggests that the two molecules are weakly bonded. In reality, the correct chemical structure is the salt C₅H₅NH⁺Cl⁻, which is more accurately named pyridinium chloride. Converting otherwise insoluble amines into their hydrochloride forms is a widely used method to render them soluble in water and acidic environments. This property is particularly advantageous for substances used in medications. Many pharmaceutical compounds are prepared as hydrochlorides to facilitate their rapid absorption in the gastrointestinal tract. Typically, hydrochlorides are absorbed within a time frame of 15 to 30 minutes. Examples of hydrochlorides in medical applications are numerous, ranging from over-the-counter sinus relief medications to anti-nausea drugs. A notable example is ondansetron hydrochloride (Zofran), which is primarily used to prevent nausea and vomiting induced by chemotherapy.
